diagrams.title: Vulnerability Management Pipeline
diagrams.subtitle: Inventory → scan → prioritization → ticket → patch → verification. Skip one step and the loop never closes.

nodes.label: Inventory
nodes.detail: Start from an asset repository: IPAM for addresses, hardware/software inventory, and CSPM for the cloud. Without an inventory, a scan covers an unknown scope and its results cannot be attributed.
nodes.exam: IPAM and CSPM are §4.3 syllabus concepts: inventory always precedes scanning.

nodes.label: Scan
nodes.detail: The scanner queries hosts and reports versions, ports, and configurations. Authenticated mode reads the actual state; unauthenticated mode gives the attacker's perspective.
nodes.exam: The scan produces a LIST, not a decision: never confuse detection with prioritization.

nodes.label: Prioritization
nodes.detail: Combine CVSS severity, exposure, asset criticality, and the existence of a known exploit or one observed in a pentest. This step turns the list into a work order.
nodes.exam: A critical on an isolated asset may come after an exposed high: reason in context.

nodes.label: Ticket & SLA
nodes.detail: Each selected vulnerability becomes a ticket with an owner, priority, and remediation SLA. The ticket is the auditable record of handling, not proof that it has been fixed.
nodes.exam: An open ticket without an owner or due date has no SLA: the exam likes this nuance.

nodes.label: Patch
nodes.detail: Apply the patch, update, hardening, service disablement, or segmentation. If patching is impossible, put a compensating control in place and document the exception.
nodes.exam: "We can't patch" never authorizes ignoring it: you need a written, approved, and dated exception.

nodes.label: Verification
nodes.detail: Re-scan the same scope with the same parameters to prove the vulnerability is gone before closing the ticket. This step closes the loop.
nodes.exam: Changing the scan method can make a finding disappear without fixing anything at all.

quiz.question: Which step turns the scanner's raw list into a prioritized work order?

diagrams.title: Authenticated vs. Unauthenticated Scan
diagrams.subtitle: Two columns, two perspectives: the actual state of the system or the view an attacker has of it.

nodes.label: Scanner
nodes.detail: The same scanner can be launched with or without credentials. The chosen mode radically changes the scope and reliability of the results, without changing the tool.
nodes.exam: The exam question is almost always about what the scanner SEES, not its speed.

nodes.label: Credentials Provided
nodes.detail: The scanner receives a dedicated read-only account. This account must be protected, rotated, and limited to the scan scope.
nodes.exam: An overly privileged scan account becomes a target itself: principle of least privilege.

nodes.label: Internal View
nodes.detail: From the inside, the scanner reads exact versions, installed patches, and local configuration. It confirms or eliminates most findings.
nodes.exam: This is the mode to remember when you want to know if a patch is ACTUALLY missing.

nodes.label: Fewer False Positives
nodes.detail: Accuracy is much better, at the cost of an account to manage and a more intrusive scan. It is the reference mode for remediation.
nodes.exam: Fewer false positives = more confidence in prioritization, not fewer vulnerabilities.

nodes.label: No Credentials
nodes.detail: The scanner hits services like any network visitor. No account is needed or disclosed.
nodes.exam: No authentication also means: no visibility into the interior.

nodes.label: Attacker View
nodes.detail: It only sees what is exposed: open ports, version banners, exposed services. This is exactly the surface an adversary can touch before any login.
nodes.exam: This is the best mode to measure external exposure, not to audit internal patches.

nodes.label: Fast but Blind
nodes.detail: A banner can lie: the service may already be patched. Unauthenticated scanning therefore generates more false positives and does not prove exploitability.
nodes.exam: False positive ≠ absent vulnerability: you must confirm before closing or escalating.

quiz.question: Which scan mode sees missing patches and the local configuration of a host?

diagrams.title: The Log Flow to the Dashboard
diagrams.subtitle: Sources → collection → normalization → correlation → alert → dashboard. A vertical stack, with timestamping across it.

nodes.label: Sources
nodes.detail: OSs, firewalls, web servers, databases, applications, and cloud services produce events in very different formats (Event Log, syslog, JSON, CSV).
nodes.exam: If a source does not emit logs, no SIEM can correlate it: coverage first, tool second.

nodes.label: Collection
nodes.detail: Agents or syslog forwarders centralize events. Transport must be reliable and timestamped: TLS and TCP are preferable to plain UDP.
nodes.exam: syslog = message protocol; collector = centralization point. Do not confuse the two.

nodes.label: Normalization
nodes.detail: Heterogeneous formats are converted into a single schema: timestamp, source, user, IP, severity. Without common fields, correlation is impossible.
nodes.exam: Normalizing does not mean deleting: the original log is retained for evidence.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.detail: The engine links events together over time: failed logins followed by success, same hash on two hosts, traffic spikes. This is the core of the SIEM.
nodes.exam: A single event is rarely an incident; correlation looks for sequences.

nodes.label: Alert
nodes.detail: When a rule matches, the SIEM creates an alert with severity and context. An uncontextualized alert becomes noise for the analyst.
nodes.exam: Alert ≠ incident: it must be triaged before triggering a response.

nodes.label: Dashboard
nodes.detail: Dashboards and metrics for the SOC: volumes, trends, open alerts, SLAs. They make visible what correlation has detected.
nodes.exam: The dashboard is for management; field verification is done in the raw log.

nodes.label: NTP Timestamping
nodes.detail: Without synchronized clocks, two logs from the same incident appear unrelated. NTP (in UTC) is the silent requirement for any reliable correlation.
nodes.exam: Think NTP whenever an exam question mentions chronology or timeline.

quiz.question: Which step converts heterogeneous formats into common fields usable by the SIEM?

diagrams.title: Alert Tuning: From Noise to Signal
diagrams.subtitle: A funnel: reduce volume before enriching, to keep only actionable alerts.

nodes.label: Noise
nodes.detail: Overly broad rules, false positives, duplicates: the analyst drowns. A SOC that treats everything at the same level treats nothing effectively.
nodes.exam: Tuning is not about disabling rules, but making them discriminating.

nodes.label: Filtering
nodes.detail: Remove duplicates, set thresholds, and allowlist known, approved behaviors. Every exclusion must be justified and reviewed.
nodes.exam: An overly broad allowlist hides a real signal: it is a compensating control, not an erasure.

nodes.label: False Positives
nodes.detail: Dismissed alerts are kept with the reason for exclusion. This record avoids reopening the same debate at every review.
nodes.exam: Documenting a false positive proves it was evaluated, not ignored.

nodes.label: Enrichment
nodes.detail: Add context: asset criticality, owner identity, threat intelligence, geolocation, history. The alert becomes a verifiable hypothesis.
nodes.exam: Enrichment precedes triage: you don't decide before having the context.

nodes.label: Signal
nodes.detail: A reduced volume of contextualized alerts remains, ready for the analyst or SOAR playbook. This is the goal of tuning.
nodes.exam: Fewer alerts + more context = more time for real incidents.

nodes.label: SOC Analyst
nodes.detail: The analyst validates the signal, opens an incident, and sends feedback on the rule. The feedback loop is what makes tuning sustainable.
nodes.exam: The human stays in the loop: tuning is an iterative process, not a one-time setting.

quiz.question: Which step adds context (IOC, asset criticality, threat intel) before qualifying the signal?

diagrams.title: Monitoring Protocols: NetFlow, SNMP, syslog, SCAP
diagrams.subtitle: Four families, four different questions. The classic trap is confusing flow, state, event, and compliance.

cells.text: Network flows (who talks to whom, when, how much)
cells.detail: Layer 3/4 metadata: source/destination IP, ports, protocol, bytes. Ideal for spotting a scan, a traffic spike, or exfiltration.
CPU, memory, interfaces, uptime. SNMP traps push a notification; polling queries at regular intervals.
Each device or application emits a message with facility and severity (0 = emergency … 7 = debug). It is the foundation of SIEM centralization.
XML framework: XCCDF for rules, OVAL for tests, CPE for naming products. Used to audit a benchmark (e.g., CIS) rather than detect in real time.
Traffic is seen in transit by the network device: a probe or flow collector (nfdump, Elastic, SIEM).
SNMP agent on the device, community string or SNMPv3 account, MIB defining readable objects.
Local agent or direct send to a syslog collector, often on UDP/514 or TCP/TLS for reliability.
A configuration scanner compares the actual state to the benchmark and produces a compliance score.
Correlate abnormal outbound volume or a host contacting many ports: this is network detection, not content analysis.
Interface down trap, CPU threshold exceeded. Complements logs: SNMP says the device is unwell, syslog says why.
Authentications, errors, configuration changes. It is the most universal source for reconstructing a timeline.
Prove that a configuration complies with policy: passwords, disabled services, encrypted settings.
NetFlow sees metadata, not packet contents. To read the payload, you need DPI or a full packet capture.

cells.text: v1/v2 read, v3 encrypts and authenticates
cells.detail: SNMPv3 adds authentication and confidentiality. Community strings in earlier versions are in cleartext.
Transport reliability is not guaranteed over UDP: prefer TCP/TLS and check timestamping.
SCAP answers 'are we configured as intended?', not 'are we being attacked right now?'.

diagrams.title: Account Lifecycle
diagrams.subtitle: Provisioning → MFA → role → access → review → deprovisioning → new need. A cycle, not a line.

nodes.label: Provisioning
nodes.detail: Account creation from an approved request, with a unique identifier, attributes, and owner. Provisioning must be tracked and automated (SCIM, IAM).
nodes.exam: Never create an account 'as needed' without a request and an owner: that's the gateway to orphan accounts.

nodes.label: MFA
nodes.detail: Add a second factor (OTP, biometrics, FIDO2 key, push). The factor must be phishing-resistant for privileged accounts.
nodes.exam: MFA ≠ 2FA: 2FA is two factors, MFA can be three or more.

nodes.label: Role
nodes.detail: Assign a role (RBAC) or attributes (ABAC) based on job function. Grant the minimum necessary, not 'just in case' rights.
nodes.exam: The role is attached to a function, not a person: that's what makes reviews possible.

nodes.label: Access
nodes.detail: The account accesses authorized resources. Privileged access can be just-in-time and expire automatically after validation.
nodes.exam: JIT = approved temporary access; it differs from permanent high-privilege access.

nodes.label: Review
nodes.detail: The owner periodically reconfirms that rights remain necessary. This is where privilege creep is detected.
nodes.exam: The review is periodic and tracked: a review without written proof does not exist for the auditor.

nodes.label: Deprovisioning
nodes.detail: Upon departure or role change, revoke sessions and tokens, disable the account, then delete data according to the retention policy.
nodes.exam: Disabling is not deleting: revoking active tokens is the step everyone forgets.

nodes.label: New Need
nodes.detail: A new need (hire, transfer, project) restarts the cycle. It is the controlled entry point that prevents ghost accounts.
nodes.exam: The cycle closes: deprovisioning feeds the next need, it is not an isolated end.

quiz.question: Which step periodically verifies that an account's rights remain appropriate?

diagrams.title: Identity Federation and SSO
diagrams.subtitle: User → IdP → SSO → SAML assertion / OAuth token → application. One identity, multiple services.

nodes.label: User
nodes.detail: The user wants to access an application without creating yet another password. Their identity remains managed by their home organization.
nodes.exam: Federation separates authentication (IdP) from authorization (application).

nodes.label: IdP
nodes.detail: The Identity Provider verifies the user (password, MFA, policy) and issues a signed assertion. It is the trusted authority.
nodes.exam: IdP = who proves identity; SP = who consumes the proof. Do not reverse them.

nodes.label: SSO
nodes.detail: Single Sign-On reuses the established session: the user does not re-enter credentials for each application.
nodes.exam: SSO improves experience AND security: fewer passwords to remember, so less reuse.

nodes.label: SAML
nodes.detail: SAML 2.0 transmits a signed identity assertion to the service provider, typically for an enterprise portal. The SP verifies the signature.
nodes.exam: SAML = federated authentication with assertion. Think 'browser + enterprise'.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.0
nodes.detail: OAuth 2.0 delegates limited access to a third-party application via tokens and consent. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on top of OAuth.
nodes.exam: OAuth = delegated authorization, not authentication. OIDC fills that exact gap.

nodes.label: Application
nodes.detail: The service provider trusts the IdP, verifies the assertion or token, and then applies its own local rights.
nodes.exam: Federating identity does not transfer authorization: the application still decides what it allows.

quiz.question: Which protocol provides a signed identity assertion to the service provider?

diagrams.title: Access Control Models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC, JIT
diagrams.subtitle: Who decides, on what basis, and with what scope? This matrix complements the account lifecycle diagram.

cells.detail: Discretionary Access Control: the owner chooses and can delegate their rights to other users, at their discretion.
Mandatory Access Control: the user, even the owner, cannot transfer a right. Labels govern access.
Role-Based Access Control: permissions are attached to a role, then users to the role. The decision is collective and predictable.
Attribute-Based Access Control: the decision is computed dynamically from attributes, without individual manual assignment.
Just-In-Time: access is granted after a request is approved, often linked to a ticket, and expires automatically.
Access control lists and inherited rights. Risk: uncontrolled propagation of privileges between users.
Confidential, secret, top secret; Bell-LaPadula-type rules (no read up, no write down). Used in MLS environments.
Accountant, developer, administrator. Easy to audit: you check membership, not every permission.
Department, clearance, file type, time, IP address, device posture. Context is part of the rule.
Limited duration, limited scope, justification required. The goal is to reduce the exposure window of privileged accounts.
A user allows a colleague to read their folder: this is DAC, because the owner decides alone.
A labeled process can only read an object at an authorized level, even if the user is root.
Add the employee to the role, remove the employee from the role: individual permissions are never touched.

cells.text: Access allowed only from corporate device during business hours
cells.detail: The same person gets or is denied access depending on device, IP, and time: this is ABAC.

cells.text: Admin access granted for 2 hours after approved ticket
cells.detail: Temporary privilege automatically revoked, often with additional MFA and session recording.
As soon as the prompt says 'the owner can grant access to a colleague', the answer is DAC.
If the prompt emphasizes 'even the owner cannot share', it is MAC. Labels enforce it.
Grouping rights by job function rather than by person is the RBAC reflex, the most common in enterprise.
Time, location, device, department: multiple dynamic attributes signal ABAC rather than RBAC.
'Time-limited access, approved then expired' is the signature of Just-In-Time.

diagrams.title: SOAR Workflow: From Alert to Feedback Loop
diagrams.subtitle: A playbook orchestrates enrichment, decision, and action — then feeds results back into the loop.

nodes.label: SIEM Alert
nodes.detail: A qualified alert or threat intelligence signal triggers the SOAR playbook. Initial context is attached to avoid starting from scratch.
nodes.exam: SOAR does not replace the SIEM: the SIEM detects, SOAR orchestrates the response.

nodes.label: Enrichment
nodes.detail: The playbook automatically queries CTI, inventory, and EDR to enrich indicators before any decision.
nodes.exam: Enriching before acting avoids blocking a legitimate or shared IP.

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.detail: The engine applies playbook conditions: severity, confidence, asset type. It chooses an action or requests human validation.
nodes.exam: A playbook is deterministic: same input, same decision — unless explicitly escalated.

nodes.label: Action
nodes.detail: Execution via connectors: IP block, host isolation, account disablement, ticket creation. Actions are bounded by guardrails.
nodes.exam: Every action must be reversible and logged: that is the condition for safe automation.

nodes.label: Feedback Loop
nodes.detail: The action's result is sent back to the playbook: success, failure, false positive. This feedback tunes the rules for the next occurrence.
nodes.exam: The feedback loop is what distinguishes a living playbook from a static script.

nodes.label: Human Escalation
nodes.detail: If confidence is low or impact is high, the playbook pauses and requests validation. Humans keep control over irreversible actions.
nodes.exam: High-impact actions (isolating production) often require approval: human-in-the-loop.

nodes.label: SOAR Log
nodes.detail: Every step of the playbook is logged: who decided, what action was taken, at what time. This is the evidence for audit and post-incident review.
nodes.exam: Without a log, you cannot explain an automated action: auditing requires this traceability.

quiz.question: Which node feeds the action's result back to enrichment to improve future decisions?

diagrams.title: Safe Automation Chain
diagrams.subtitle: Trigger → logic → guardrail → execution → verification. Automation without a guardrail is a risk, not a gain.

nodes.label: Trigger
nodes.detail: An event launches the automation: webhook, schedule, new alert, or state change. The trigger must be authenticated.
nodes.exam: An unauthenticated webhook lets anyone trigger your actions: that is a major risk.

nodes.label: Logic
nodes.detail: Logic decides the course of action based on conditions: thresholds, asset type, severity. It must be simple and testable.
nodes.exam: An ambiguous condition produces unpredictable actions: logic is documented and tested.

nodes.label: Guardrail
nodes.detail: The guardrail bounds the action: maximum scope, host count, time window, dual approval. It prevents automation from stepping outside its boundaries.
nodes.exam: This is THE node to cite when a question asks how to 'prevent an error from spreading to the entire fleet'.

nodes.label: Execution
nodes.detail: The action is performed via an API or script with a dedicated, least-privilege account and credentials stored in a vault.
nodes.exam: Never hardcode credentials: it's a classic in code review and on the exam.

nodes.label: Verification
nodes.detail: Re-read the state after the action: is the IP really blocked? Is the account actually disabled? A technically successful action can have no business effect.
nodes.exam: Verifying means comparing expected and observed — not just checking the API return code.

nodes.label: Rollback
nodes.detail: If verification fails or the effect is too broad, undo the action and restore the known state. Every automated action must be reversible.
nodes.exam: Irreversible automation without validation is a wrong exam answer, even if it is fast.

nodes.label: Audit
nodes.detail: Retain inputs, decision, action, and result. This log enables auditing, tuning, and recovery in case of an incident.
nodes.exam: Auditing makes automation explainable: essential for compliance and post-incident review.

quiz.question: Which element prevents an automation from acting outside a scope or without explicit validation?

diagrams.title: Incident Response Preparedness
diagrams.subtitle: Charter, roles, playbooks, tools, training, exercises, and communication: train before the incident.

nodes.label: IR Charter
nodes.detail: The charter defines who is responsible, what the incident declaration criteria are, and how far the team can act (isolation, shutdown, communication).
nodes.exam: Without a charter, the team hesitates at the critical moment: authority must be decided beforehand.

nodes.label: Roles
nodes.detail: Designate a lead, analysts, a communications lead, and a legal representative, with backups and an on-call directory.
nodes.exam: Always plan a backup: preparedness also covers the primary person's absence.

nodes.label: Playbooks
nodes.detail: Ransomware, phishing, account compromise: each scenario has its procedure, decision criteria, and contacts. A runbook is more technical, a playbook more decision-oriented.
nodes.exam: The playbook reduces improvisation under pressure: that is the number one goal of preparedness.

nodes.label: Tools
nodes.detail: Verified access to EDR, SIEM, forensic imaging, and isolation tools. Access is tested before the incident, not during.
nodes.exam: A tool whose password is only in the primary admin's head is unavailable in a crisis.

nodes.label: Training
nodes.detail: Ongoing team training and business awareness: knowing how to recognize and report an incident is part of preparedness.
nodes.exam: Training also applies to users: human detection remains a key alert source.

nodes.label: Exercises
nodes.detail: Tabletop exercises followed by technical simulations. They reveal playbook blind spots, outdated contacts, and stalled decisions.
nodes.exam: Tabletops test decisions and communication; simulations test tools. Both are complementary.

nodes.label: Communication
nodes.detail: Redundant crisis channels, list of internal contacts, legal, HR, vendors, and authorities, with pre-approved message templates.
nodes.exam: A crisis channel that depends on the internal network may be unavailable during an attack: plan a fallback.

quiz.question: Which element defines the team's authority and scope before even writing playbooks?

diagrams.title: Containment Decision Tree
diagrams.subtitle: Isolate? Preserve evidence? Notify? Eradicate? A decision tree, not a single recipe.

nodes.label: Incident Detected
nodes.detail: The alert has been qualified: we have an initial scope, severity, and initial time horizon. Decision-making starts here.
nodes.exam: Do not confuse detection and containment: triage always precedes action.

nodes.label: Should We Isolate?
nodes.detail: Assess the active threat, system criticality, and cost of an outage. If the host is actively destroying evidence, isolation may take priority.
nodes.exam: The decision depends on business context: isolating a production server does not have the same cost as isolating a workstation.

nodes.label: Preserve Evidence
nodes.detail: If possible before isolation, capture volatile memory, connections, and logs: the order of volatility dictates the collection order.
nodes.exam: Powering off a machine destroys RAM: it is an irreversible loss of evidence.

nodes.label: Isolate Host
nodes.detail: Network disconnection or EDR quarantine to stop propagation, while keeping the machine powered on if acquisition is needed.
nodes.exam: Isolate ≠ power off: network quarantine cuts communications without destroying memory.

nodes.label: Notify
nodes.detail: Notify stakeholders per the charter: CISO, asset owner, legal, communications, and sometimes authorities or customers.
nodes.exam: Notification follows the charter and legal obligations: it is not decided on a whim.

nodes.label: Eradicate
nodes.detail: Remove malware, rotate compromised credentials, rebuild from a clean image, and patch the entry vulnerability.
nodes.exam: Cleaning without changing passwords leaves the attacker persistent access: rotation is essential.

nodes.label: Controlled Recovery
nodes.detail: Restore service with heightened monitoring and verification that the entry vector is closed. Watch for recurrence.
nodes.exam: Recovery without heightened monitoring risks leaving an undetected backdoor.

nodes.label: Document
nodes.detail: Every decision, timestamp, and owner is recorded. This timeline will be used for the PIR, audit, and any legal proceedings.
nodes.exam: Document during the incident, not after: human memory fades quickly under pressure.

quiz.question: Before isolating a machine, what should be preserved if acquisition is possible?

diagrams.title: Post-Incident Loop: From PIR to Playbooks
diagrams.subtitle: Post-incident review → root cause → lessons → playbook updates → sharing → action tracking.

nodes.label: PIR
nodes.detail: Calm meeting with all parties: factual reconstruction of the timeline, without blame. Rely on logs, not memories.
nodes.exam: The PIR is a blameless review: that is a prerequisite for honest feedback.

nodes.label: Root Cause
nodes.detail: Look for the underlying cause, not just the symptom: why the patch was missing, why the alert was ignored, why the contact was outdated.
nodes.exam: Treating only the symptom guarantees recurrence: the exam expects the root cause.

nodes.label: Lessons Learned
nodes.detail: Formalize what worked well and poorly, with assigned corrective actions: owner, due date, success criteria.
nodes.exam: A lesson without an assigned action or due date remains just a lesson: it must become a task.

nodes.label: Update
nodes.detail: Playbooks, SIEM rules, controls, and policies are updated to incorporate feedback. This is where experience becomes reusable.
nodes.exam: This step closes the loop with preparedness: post-incident feeds the next exercise.

nodes.label: Sharing
nodes.detail: A summary is shared with relevant teams and leadership. Sensitive details are filtered according to the communication policy.
nodes.exam: Share lessons without exposing exploit details: distribution is controlled.

nodes.label: Tracking
nodes.detail: Measure detection and response times (MTTD/MTTR) and track corrective actions until verified closure.
nodes.exam: An action is only finished when its effect is verified, not when the box is checked.

quiz.question: Which step turns lessons learned into reusable procedures for the next crisis?

diagrams.title: Evidence Volatility Pyramid
diagrams.subtitle: From most volatile to most stable: collect what disappears fastest first. Collection order = order of volatility.

nodes.label: Registers / Cache
nodes.detail: CPU registers, cache, and queues: nanoseconds to seconds. In practice, they are lost as soon as you touch the machine.
nodes.exam: This is the top of the pyramid: if the prompt says 'immediately', think memory and CPU.

nodes.label: RAM
nodes.detail: Processes, encryption keys, code injections, system tables. Memory acquisition is done before any power-off.
nodes.exam: A disk image does NOT contain RAM: a separate memory acquisition is required.

nodes.label: Network Connections
nodes.detail: Established connections, ARP table, DNS cache, routes. They change within minutes and often reveal active C2 or exfiltration.
nodes.exam: netstat / ss and NetFlow streams should be captured early: a closed session does not come back.

nodes.label: Processes
nodes.detail: Active processes, handles, loaded DLLs, threads. Their true state exists only in memory and must be captured with it.
nodes.exam: Fileless malware exists only there: RAM is the only source that shows it.

nodes.label: Disk
nodes.detail: Files, metadata, logs, unallocated space. Stable, but modifiable: work on an image with write blockers.
nodes.exam: Always acquire a bit-by-bit image and hash it: never analyze the original directly.

nodes.label: Logs
nodes.detail: Event Logs, syslog, application logs. Central logs are more reliable than local logs, which the attacker can erase.
nodes.exam: A skilled attacker erases local logs: also collect from the SIEM.

nodes.label: Backups
nodes.detail: Tapes, snapshots, off-site archives: the most stable and oldest. They allow pre-incident comparison and restoration.
nodes.exam: Base of the pyramid: useful for restoration and history, but too late for volatile evidence.

quiz.question: Which source should be collected first according to the order of volatility?

diagrams.title: Evidence Sources and Unified Timeline
diagrams.subtitle: Host, network, cloud, and EDR converge toward correlation, then a horizontal, timestamped timeline.

nodes.label: Host Logs
nodes.detail: Logins, executions, configuration changes. Most universal source, but vulnerable to erasure by the attacker.
nodes.exam: Local logs are evidence; centralized logs are a more reliable copy.

nodes.label: Network Logs
nodes.detail: Flows, DNS queries, outbound connections. They show communications even when the compromised host no longer cooperates.
nodes.exam: DNS is a goldmine: a newly resolved domain often reveals C2.

nodes.label: Cloud Logs
nodes.detail: API calls, IAM changes, storage object access. The cloud requires explicitly enabled and centralized logging.
nodes.exam: In the cloud, 'who called which API and from which IP' often replaces the host log.

nodes.label: EDR Telemetry
nodes.detail: EDR records execution, injections, connections, and memory artifacts. It fills the gap of classic logs on fileless attacks.
nodes.exam: EDR = behavioral visibility on the endpoint; it complements the SIEM, it does not replace it.

nodes.label: UTC Timestamping
nodes.detail: Without synchronized clocks, the four sources cannot be aligned. Time zone and UTC must be normalized before correlation.
nodes.exam: A drift of a few minutes can cause you to miss the entire attack chain.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.detail: Link sources by common entities: user, IP, hash, hostname. Correlation turns four independent streams into a single story.
nodes.exam: Correlating means looking for the link, not adding up log volumes.

nodes.label: Timeline
nodes.detail: The timeline orders events from oldest to newest with their sources. It is the backbone of the investigation report.
nodes.exam: A timeline must state the source and confidence level of each event.

nodes.label: Report
nodes.detail: Summary with scope, chronology, impacts, cited evidence, and recommendations. Facts are separated from hypotheses.
nodes.exam: An investigation report always separates what is proven from what is assumed.

quiz.question: Which source captures endpoint execution and memory at a behavioral level?

diagrams.title: Evidence Chain of Custody
diagrams.subtitle: Collection → hashing → sealing → register → transfer → analysis → report → storage. Every hand is tracked.

nodes.label: Collection
nodes.detail: Bit-by-bit acquisition of the source, with write blockers and scope documentation. Collection follows the order of volatility.
nodes.exam: Acquiring the original alters the evidence: work on a forensic copy.

nodes.label: Hashing
nodes.detail: Compute a cryptographic digest of the image. An identical hash before and after transfer proves nothing was modified.
nodes.exam: The hash does not prove authenticity, but integrity: it detects any modification, even unintentional.

nodes.label: Sealing
nodes.detail: The medium is placed in a sealed anti-static bag, with label, unique number, date, and collector's signature.
nodes.exam: A broken or unnumbered seal makes the evidence contestable, even if the hash is good.

nodes.label: Register
nodes.detail: Every transfer is recorded: who hands over, who receives, when, where, and why. The register establishes unbroken continuity.
nodes.exam: Chain of custody is a documented sequence of hands: a gap in the chain weakens the evidence.

nodes.label: Transfer
nodes.detail: Transport to the lab or analyst, with encryption if the transfer is digital and a signed receipt.
nodes.exam: Transferring an unencrypted image by email is a breach of confidentiality and traceability.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.detail: The analyst works on a copy of the image, recalculates the hash, and records tools and methods so the analysis is reproducible.
nodes.exam: Recalculating the hash upon opening proves the analysis is performed on the sealed evidence.

nodes.label: Report
nodes.detail: Conclusions are supported by specific artifacts with evidence references, method used, and limitations of the analysis.
nodes.exam: A forensic report cites the evidence and method: a claim without reference is not admissible.

nodes.label: Storage
nodes.detail: Evidence is stored according to the retention policy and legal obligations, in a controlled environment accessible only to authorized personnel.
nodes.exam: Destroying evidence before the end of retention can turn negligence into obstruction.
